# Introduction

Computational tools are at the heart of modern palaeontology. From cleaning datasets to running complex analyses, software underpins much of what we do.

This module introduces you to [palaeoverse](https://palaeoverse.palaeoverse.org), an R package developed to help you get your palaeontological data into the right shape for analyses and keep your code clear.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this module, you will be able to:

- Install and load palaeoverse, and locate its documentation, vignettes, and resources
- Understand the design and potential applications of palaeoverse
- Apply palaeoverse functions to explore, prepare, and visualise fossil occurrence data
- Identify palaeoverse functions for use in your own research workflow

## Pre-requisites and Related Modules

You should be comfortable with basic R (data frames, functions, installing packages). Experience with fossil occurrence data, for example from the [Paleobiology Database (PBDB)](https://paleobiodb.org/#/), is also helpful but not required.

If needed, you can refer to our [R Basics]() module. **LINK NEEDS ADDING**

## Why use palaeoverse

Palaeobiological analyses rarely go straight from raw data to results. Most begin with routine but essential tasks, such as checking taxonomic names, binning occurrences in time or space, and reconstructing palaeogeographic distributions, which are often rewritten from scratch for every project. *palaeoverse* aims to stop us reinventing the wheel by making this work reusable, reproducible, and readable. It replaces long, bespoke scripts with a few clear lines of code, uses consistent function names, arguments and outputs so that scripts are easy to follow and share, and provides well-documented, tested and peer-reviewed functions that are transparent and robust.

# Design

palaeoverse is built around a small set of principles that shape how functions look and behave:

- Dataframe orientated: most functions expect an occurrence `data.frame` as the input
- Modular: each function does one job well, you can use a single function in isolation or chain several together
- Flexible: functions are not tied to a single data source (e.g. Paleobiology Database), column names are generally arguments rather than fixed requirements, so you can use data from any source with ease
- Transparent and reproducible: all code is documented and open source, so it can be reviewed by anyone
- Well documented: every function has a help page with worked examples to help users get started
- Community driven: developed openly, with peer-review from fellow researchers, and users encouraged to suggest features, report bugs, and contribute

# Design

Three design choices shape how palaeoverse functions look and behave.

## Built around occurrence data

Most functions in palaeoverse take an occurrence `data.frame` as input, so they slot straight into the way many palaeobiologists already store their data.

::: {.callout-note}
## What is an occurrence dataset?

In an occurrence dataset, each row is a single record of something present at a particular place and time. That "something" is usually a taxon, but it does not have to be. For example, in the in-built `reefs` dataset, each row is a fossil reef rather than a species.

Occurrence data typically include columns describing:

- *Taxonomy* (e.g. accepted name, genus, and family)
- *Age* (e.g. maximum and minimum ages or named intervals)
- *Location* (e.g. longitude and latitude)
- *Additional context* (formation, collection, or reference)

It could look something a little like this:

  | occurrence_no   | accepted_name   | max_ma   | min_ma   | lng      | lat     | …     |
  | --------------: | --------------: | -------: | -------: | -------: | ------: | ----: |
  |           40163 |      Crocodylia |     59.2 |       56 |   −74.68 |   39.97 |     … |
  |           40167 |     Gavialoidea |     59.2 |       56 |   −74.68 |   39.97 |     … |
  |           40168 |     Gavialoidea |     59.2 |       56 |   −74.68 |   39.97 |     … |
  |               … |               … |        … |        … |        … |       … |     … |
:::

## Modular

Each function in palaeoverse does one job well. Use one on its own, or chain several together into a full workflow.

```{r}
#| label: modular
#| eval: false

# Load library
library(palaeoverse)
# Get example data
data(tetrapods)
# Get time bins
bins <- time_bins(interval = "Phanerozoic", rank = "stage")
# Bin data temporally
tetrapods |>
  bin_time(bins = bins, method = "mid")
```

## Flexible

Functions in palaeoverse are not tied to a single source such as the Paleobiology Database. Column names are generally arguments rather than fixed requirements, so data from any source can be used with ease.

```{r}
#| label: flexible
#| eval: false

# Load library
library(palaeoverse)
# Get example data
data(tetrapods)
# Get time bins
bins <- time_bins(interval = "Phanerozoic", rank = "stage")
# Bin data temporally
tetrapods |>
  bin_time(bins = bins, method = "mid")
```

# Applications

palaeoverse can be used for a wide range of applications, including:

Cleaning and standardising occurrence data (e.g. checking taxonomic names and removing duplicates):

```{r}
#| label: check-names
#| eval: true

# Load library
library(palaeoverse)
# Get example data
data(tetrapods)
# Check for potential misspellings
tax_check(tetrapods, name = "genus")
```

Binning occurrences into temporal and spatial units (e.g. for analyses of diversity and biogeography):

```{r}
#| label: bin-space
#| eval: true

# Load library
library(palaeoverse)
# Get example data
data(tetrapods)
# Bin data into equal-area hexagonal cells
bin_space(tetrapods, spacing = 250)
```

Estimating the position of organisms at time of deposition (i.e. palaeogeographic reconstruction):

```{r}
#| label: palaeorotate
#| eval: false

# Load library
library(palaeoverse)
# Get example data
data(tetrapods)
# Add midpoint age
tetrapods$mid_ma <- (tetrapods$max_ma + tetrapods$min_ma) / 2
# Bin data into equal-area hexagonal cells
palaeorotate(tetrapods, age = "mid_ma", model = "PALEOMAP")
```

Summarising taxa, such as estimating temporal and geographic ranges:

```{r}
#| label: temporal-range
#| eval: true

# Load library
library(palaeoverse)
# Get example data
data(tetrapods)
# Estimate temporal range of taxa
tetrapods |>
  # Drop NAs
  subset(!is.na(order)) |>
  # Plot temporal range
  tax_range_time(name = "order", plot = TRUE)
```

These steps can feed into a wide range of downstream analyses, including diversity dynamics, macroevolution, macroecology and biogeography.

::: {.callout-note}
## Where does palaeoverse fit?

Think of palaeoverse as the bridge between raw occurrence data and the analytical methods you want to apply.
:::

# Installation

To install the current release of [palaeoverse](https://palaeoverse.palaeoverse.org) from CRAN (recommended), use:

```{r}
#| label: install-palaeoverse
#| eval: false

install.packages("palaeoverse")
```

If the development version is preferred, first install the [remotes](https://remotes.r-lib.org/) package, and then use `install_github()` to install [palaeoverse](https://github.com/palaeoverse/palaeoverse/) directly from GitHub:

```{r}
#| label: install-remotes
#| eval: false

install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("palaeoverse/palaeoverse")
```

Now you are able to load palaeoverse:

```{r}
#| label: load-palaeoverse

library(palaeoverse)
```

# Getting help

Everyone gets stuck with using new (and familiar) tools from time-to-time, and knowing where to look is one of the most useful skills you can develop. As with most packages, *palaeoverse* has several layers of support, from built-in documentation to wider community support.

The *palaeoverse* [website](https://palaeoverse.palaeoverse.org) hosts the full function documentation, vignettes and updates on new releases. It is searchable and can be easier to browse than the help pages in R.

![You can see all available functions and their documentation via the package's dedicated website [reference guide](https://palaeoverse.palaeoverse.org/reference/index.html).](img/palaeoverse-reference.png)

If you are familiar with GitHub, you can also check existing issues within the dedicated [repository](https://github.com/palaeoverse/palaeoverse/), as someone may already have asked your question. If you cannot find an answer to your question, you can open an [issue](https://github.com/palaeoverse/palaeoverse/issues) on GitHub (see [best practises](https://reprex.tidyverse.org/articles/reprex-dos-and-donts.html)).

::: {.callout-tip}
GitHub can be a *scary* place if you are not familiar with it. So, you can also reach out by [email](mailto:info@palaeoverse.org) if you are facing difficulties or join our [Zulip](https://palaeoverse.org/zulip/join-zulip/), and raise a topic.
:::
